chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hanan ibn Sudeyr, who said:

My father and I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and said to him, 'May Allah make us your ransom! We have companions among the Christians, and we go to them, and they slaughter for us poultry, chicks, and young goats. Can we eat them?' He said, 'Do not eat them, and do not go near them, for they say upon their slaughters something that I do not like for you to eat.'

He (the narrator) said, 'So when we arrived in Kufa, one of them invited us, so we refused to go. He said, 'What is the matter with you? You used to come to us, then you left it today?' We said, 'A knowledgeable one among us (peace be upon him) forbade us, and he claimed that you say upon your slaughters something that he does not like for us to eat.' He said, 'Who is this knowledgeable one? By Allah, he is the most knowledgeable of the people, and the most knowledgeable one whom Allah created. By Allah, he spoke the truth; we say, 'In the name of the Messiah (peace be upon him)'.'

key_terms.بِسْمِ الْمَسِيح: In the name of the Messiah
key_terms.خُلْطَاء: companions or neighbors living in proximity

ai.seo_question: Why did the Shia Imams forbid eating meat slaughtered by Christians?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the Shia juristic principle of 'takhassus' (specificity), where the general permissibility of People of the Book's meat is restricted by their specific liturgical practices. The Imam’s prohibition stems from the Christians' invocation of 'Bismillah al-Masih' (In the name of the Messiah), which introduces a distinct theological element differing from the pure Tawhid of Islam. This distinction underscores the importance of not only the slaughterer's identity but also the spiritual content of their ritual invocation.
